title: George Lewis's tone and the Zeb Linares contest
summary: George's mastery and tone; a contest of Jack Carey's and Chris Kelly's bands with Zeb.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Well, tell me about George Lewis at that time. What did, what did he sound like saying that?

George sounded good. George was really, I mean, I didn't know, George just mastered that horn and he had such a wonderful tone, you know? And, uh, everybody admired George's playing. And that's why George got to be known, you know, so much like he did because he had a nice tone and, uh, well, I mean, he was real active. I mean, active. He was great. Because any time, uh, you get on the, uh, I see one time we had a, uh, contest with two bands. Well, I was waking with, uh, Jack Carey band and, uh, George was with Chris Kelly band. And, but we had, uh, this boy, uh, Zeb Linares. I don't know if you ever heard talk of Zeb. Zeb was playing with Jack Carey band, which I wore too. And, uh, George, George was playing with Chris Kelly. But I mean, George played so much clarin'. That's how Zeb got, you know, just a bad feeling. He knew he couldn't come up to the stand like George did, you know? So, and, uh, everybody, well, don't worry about that. See, everybody's better and, you know, good and betters all over. Yeah, right.
Yeah. But he, did he play pretty much the same style then? Do you think George was his favorite later when he started to make records?
George? Yeah. George was on the same style. Yeah. George didn't change much at all.
Do you think he got any better?
Oh, yeah, he got better. Yeah.
George got a whole lot better than he was.
In fact, he always worked good. I mean, you know, the more you play your instrument, the more you get used to it, you know? Because you'll start his tone and fingering and all that, you know?
